A1.justification: Despite changes in title and scope, both PDFs describe the same CLIP/OpenCLIP bias audit on FairFace and PATA. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original zero-shot bias measurements on FairFace and PATA, including multilingual experiments, in Tables 1–8 and accompanying figures.

after.justification: v3 reports empirical bias measurements and model/corpus comparisons on FairFace and PATA in Tables 1–3 and Figures 1–4.

M1.justification: Both versions audit existing CLIP-family checkpoints through zero-shot image–text comparisons. No new architecture, training algorithm or mitigation component is established; removed multilingual checkpoints concern comparison coverage, while added mathematical and inference descriptions concern metrics and documentation.

E1.justification: v3 removes evaluation in Finnish, Turkish and Farsi, substantially narrowing v1's multilingual coverage to English. FairFace, PATA and the criminal/non-human, communion and agency probes remain.

E2.justification: v1's comparisons include mCLIP with XLM-Roberta at B/32 and L/14, and LaBSE at L/14, alongside monolingual CLIP. These multilingual comparators disappear from v3's reported results. Six identifiable monolingual CLIP/OpenCLIP configurations remain; the seventh checkpoint mentioned in v3's text has no identifiable results row.

E3.justification: v3 substantially revises the stated crime protocol to demographic-filled criminal/animal prompts, specifies 10,954 balanced FairFace validation images instead of v1's 10,000, and introduces cross-trait mean summaries. These are reported protocol revisions: the retained appendix still contains the same 45 prompts, and v3 elsewhere still says 10,000 images, so the implemented prompt protocol and any rerunning remain unresolved.

E4.justification: v3 removes the analyses testing whether multilingual text encoders and absence of grammatical gender suppress bias, including v1 Section 4.2.3 and Figures 11–12. The illustrative prediction cases in v1 Figure 1 also disappear. Retained model/data sensitivity comparisons receive new delta and cross-trait summaries in v3 Tables 2–3 rather than new robustness experiments.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without stated statistical uncertainty. v3 Figure 4 adds whiskers labeled as 95% bootstrap confidence intervals; Figure 1's caption also claims such intervals. Bootstrap resampling counts, seeds and repeated model-run counts remain unspecified, making this a limited reporting addition.

E6.justification: Numerous retained results change: FairFace CLIP L/14 negative agency is 78% in v1 Table 4 versus 20% in v3 Table 1, and its criminal mean racial skew changes from 1.81 to 5.28. Multilingual results and maximum racial-skew entries disappear, while Tables 2–3 add numerical deltas and averages. These are revised reports, not established same-protocol performance improvements.

T1.justification: v3 Section 3.4 introduces an explicit group-conditioned association definition based on mean cosine similarity. The original pairwise Max Skew formula remains unchanged. The contrastive-loss equation supplies background exposition, and neither version contains theoretical propositions or proofs.

C1.justification: v3 removes multilingual bias transfer as a central contribution and claims a first controlled study disentangling encoder size, corpus scale and composition. It replaces v1's qualified scaling findings with more categorical family-specific claims, including doubling OpenCLIP's gender bias and a corpus-dependent demographic trade-off. The general warning that scaling does not ensure fairness remains.

C2.justification: Cross-lingual and grammatical-gender interpretations are replaced by stronger assertions about corpus composition, gradients and majority-group updates causing bias. v3 adds ensembling/calibration suggestions and specific limitations concerning intersectional coverage, prompt sensitivity, newer architectures and possible pretraining-data overlap. These extend beyond relocating v1's limitations discussion.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents 224/336-pixel input resolutions, checkpoint-specific temperature, absence of test-time augmentation, an A100 40 GB GPU and inference under thirty minutes. The exact prompt appendix is retained. Code availability remains ambiguous: release claims in the abstract coexist with Section 3.5's promise of release upon publication, without an access location.

R1.justification: The multilingual/cross-lingual related-work thread is replaced by expanded bias-measurement, mitigation and scaling discussions, including MODSCAN, BENDVLM, VHELM and additional scaling studies. Positioning shifts toward a claimed first controlled separation of architectural and corpus factors. These cited mitigation methods are not newly evaluated baselines.

P1.justification: The title and most main-text prose are extensively rewritten. Results move from task-based organization to sections organized by experimental factor, related work is restructured, and limitations become a separate section. The prompt appendix remains substantially verbatim under a new appendix label.

P2.justification: The single-column ACM layout becomes a two-column layout. v1 Tables 1, 3 and 4 are consolidated into v3 Table 1; new color-coded delta tables and bar charts replace the earlier scatterplot presentation, and multilingual figures and example images disappear. Several new captions misdescribe their displays: Figure 3 calls negative delta bars absolute skew values.

improvement.justification: v3 improves organization and adds inference details and some confidence intervals, but substantially weakens the reliability of its central analysis. Unlike v1's qualified scaling conclusion, v3 Section 5 says every OpenCLIP bias metric worsens with more data, although Table 1 shows PATA L/14 crime gender skew falling from 3.10 to 1.24. New Table 2 reports a +0.96 FairFace OpenCLIP@400M size delta despite corresponding Table 1 values of 0.45 and 2.18. These central inconsistencies, together with misleading figure captions, outweigh the documentation gains.
